newsitem.title: UK: Guinness fires salvo in legal wrangle.
newsitem.headline: Guinness fires salvo in legal wrangle.

text.p: French luxury goods group LVMH Moet Hennessey Louis Vuitton S.A. on Friday announced it would take drinks group Guinness to an arbitration hearing, prompting Guinness to claim the LVMH case lacked any legal basis.

The LVMH decision marks the first step in what is viewed in the drinks industry as an increasingly bitter legal wrangle which threatens to hold up a proposed 24 billion pounds merger between Guinness and Grand Metropolitan Plc.

"Guinness is clear that LVMH's claim that the proposed merger of GrandMet and Guinness would constitute a 'control event' lacks any legal basis, and is confident that the ICC (International Chamber of Commerce) arbitration will find accordingly," said Guinness in a statement.
Earlier LVMH, the largest shareholder in Guinness with a 14.2 percent stake, submitted a request for arbitration to the ICC claiming that the merger constitutes a change of control at Guinness.

Commenting on the announcement Guinness chairman Tony Greener said, "We are not surprised by this latest development; we are confident of the outcome and that the timetable for the merger will be unaffected."

LVMH argues that the proposed 24 billion pound ($39.1 billion) merger between Guinness and GrandMet would trigger a "control event" under terms it agreed with Guinness, enabling LVMH to operate its joint ventures with Guinness independently.
LVMH also argues that the terms would allow it to market Guinness brands in key markets like the United States and the Far East for up to 10 years.

LVMH voted against the merger on the grounds that it would create a food and drinks giant with few synergies and fail to increase shareholder value. LVMH chairman Bernard Arnault argues that only the wines and spirits of the two groups are complementary and sees more value in merging the drinks activities of LVMH, Guinness and possibly GrandMet.
Guinness argues that that the merger does not constitute the kind of "control event" allowing LVMH to exercise the rights because it is a merger rather than a take-over of Guinness by GrandMet.
"This view has been unequivocally supported by opinions that Guinness has obtained from independent legal counsel in relevant jurisdictions, including France," said Guinness in the statement.

Under the terms of the proposed merger Guinness shareholders will retain their shares in Guinness which is renamed GMG Brands, while GrandMet shareholders receive one GMG Brands share for every one GrandMet share.

If the deal takes place GrandMet shares will be delisted and the name Guinness changed to GMG Brands. The GMG Brands board will be made up of five directors drawn from each company and a joint chairman from each side. ($ = 0.613 British Pounds)
